title: Wait, you actually clicked on this?
text:
I used to go on special trips with my mom to a Japanese supermarket in a suburb of Chicago, and would spend hours at a time in the stationery section, exploring all manner of pens and pencils.
I started collecting pencils, first. I liked all of the different mechanisms. Auto-rotating lead, shake-to-advance, twisting erasers. From there, I moved on to pens.

title: Wait, you actually clicked on this?
text:
My collection






I own a ballpoint Cross Bailey, an Ohto Liberty (in UCLA colors, of course), a Caran d’Ache ballpoint, and a Kaweco sport (with my favorite green ink) to name a few of my pens. As far as pencils, my two favorites are the Tombow MONO Graph and the UNI \(\alpha\)-gel switch.
As a math major, my obsession with handwriting doesn’t end there, either! I love a good chalkboard, and pretty much anything to do with handwriting, notation, or the art of putting ideas into the physical world.

title: Overview
text:
My name is Mario Truong, and I am an undergraduate at UCLA. I plan on pursuing graduate school in order to go into the field of operations research. I am drawn to this field as a result of its wide reaching impact in healthcare, energy, and urban planning. Furthermore, I always seek solid justification in my decision-making process, and operations research caters to precisely that—scientific decision making.
Scroll down to learn more about me, or navigate to the about section.





In Utah, on the way to UCLA


















Where I’m From
Being from Wisconsin informs my perspective on the environments in which I find myself. The contrast of being mixed and growing up in the cultural homogeneity of my midwestern town emphasized the importance of cultural diversity. While my community may have been culturally uniform, its political variety taught me from a young age how to create productive conversation with those who disagree with me. Going to school in Los Angeles, I now understand a wider range of the American identity.

text:
Projects






Design, Build, Fly at UCLA
I am a member of the aerodynamics subteam, where I conduct computational fluid dynamics simulations, post processing data analysis, and trade studies. Learning how to use software such as SimScale and XFLR, as well as being part of a team of engineers taught me the effective communication and collaborations skills required of engineers.























TraffiX
I worked with two other team members to code a traffic simulation package. Presenting this project to others required describing a technical model in intuitive terms, meaning this project challenged both my communication and coding skills. We worked with NetworkX and integrated OSMNX to glean real-world data to simulate for this project. Overall, learning how to build a model from scratch taught me how to apply careful observation about the world around us to a mathematical problem.









NASA and the Wisconsin Space Grant Consortium’s Aerospace Jam
I worked on a drone for a competition inspired by NASA’s Ingenuity mission. I coded an arduino to control a claw, ultrasonic sensor, and an air pump via an Android app. Competition day was nerve-wracking, but my teammates and I persevered and had an amazing experience designing, building, and testing our drone.

title: Mario Truong
section: I can juggle 5 at a time.
text:
I can juggle 5 at a time.






I first learned how to juggle from a book I got for Christmas. I started to lose interest until my sister also got into juggling. Then, my competitive brotherly instincts kicked in—I needed to beat her at juggling.
The rest is history. I have attended international juggling festivals, the (perpetually 47th) annual MadFest, and am the treasurer of my local juggling club. As the treasurer, I am charged with handling the club funds accumulated from our massive income stream (change found on the ground). Juggling is fun, and I encourage anyone interested to learn!
